questions.prompt: Match each fault to its fix.
questions.explain: Every fault leaves a gap or a missing push.

questions.prompt: A torch doesn't work. You swap in new cells and it still doesn't work. What should you check next?
questions.explain: Test one part at a time: the bulb's filament and the switch contacts.

questions.prompt: How can you tell which leg of an LED goes towards the + terminal?
questions.explain: The longer leg (the anode) connects towards +.

questions.prompt: A circuit has one cell and one LED, the right way round, but it doesn't glow. What is the most likely reason?
options: The LED needs about 2 V, but one cell gives only 1.5 V
questions.explain: Adding a second cell (3 V) makes it glow.

questions.explain: A working circuit needs a complete conducting loop and a net push from the cells.

questions.prompt: Describe a step-by-step method a detective could use to find the fault in ANY simple circuit that doesn't work.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) Check the cells: are they working and facing the same way? 2) Check the switch is closed. 3) Check every connection is tight and every part in the loop is a conductor. 4) Check the bulb's filament or the LED's direction, and whether it has enough voltage. 5) Test one change at a time and observe the result, so you know which change fixed it.
rubric: Covers cells, switch, connections/materials and the bulb/LED
Changes one thing at a time
questions.explain: Criterion C: a logical troubleshooting procedure.

questions.prompt: Why does changing only ONE thing at a time help when fixing a circuit?
options: You know exactly which change fixed the problem
questions.explain: This is the same idea as a fair test.
